character_and_relationship_context:
Aminata Diallo is a young woman living in a rented room on the outskirts of Bamako. She rises before dawn, uses a kerosene lamp, and fetches water from a communal stand two blocks away. She works six days a week as the youngest and only woman on a construction crew. Her master mason, Sékou, who lost two fingers to a faulty crane, calls her "la petite comptable" because she recalculates load-bearing estimates in her head. She does not laugh at his teasing; she simply nods and checks the plumb line. Her habit of double-checking is a reflex from watching her mother lose a market stall to a miscalculated loan. Her mother died when Aminata was twelve. She counts everything: bricks, cost of rice, weeks until her next accounting exam. She keeps a notebook inside her shirt and hides an emergency fund under a loose floorboard, the same amount each month, never touched. At night after ten hours of hauling cement and stacking blocks, she studies by the lamp until her eyes burn. Her accounting course is at a community center on the other side of the city; she cannot afford the bus fare both ways, so she walks. She walks past stalls, keeping her eyes on the ground, counting her steps. She is saving for a proper room with running water where her younger sister can live with her and go to school, but she does not speak of this aloud because plans that are spoken become plans borrowed against. Her coworkers respect her silence and precision. They do not know that she watched her father sell his tools to pay for her mother's funeral and that he never held a trowel again. She holds her trowel every day and checks every measurement twice, because she has learned that the only thing you can trust is what you have counted yourself.

Her older maternal cousin Fatoumata, a few years senior, married young and lives nearby. Fatoumata occasionally checked on Aminata after her mother died, bringing food, but also asks for help with family events because she knows Aminata is reliable. Aminata feels a quiet obligation to Fatoumata, who is one of the few relatives who acknowledges her work as a builder without condescension.

When coworkers invite her to evening gatherings, she consistently declines to study. She has never taken a day off from the construction site except when ill. She once agreed to help her aunt prepare for a wedding, then spent the night catching up on lost study time, a pattern she found exhausting. She avoids spoken commitments that could conflict with her savings schedule.
objective_situation: On a Sunday afternoon, Aminata’s cousin Fatoumata visits her rented room. Fatoumata is organizing a naming ceremony for her newborn next week and asks Aminata to help prepare traditional dishes the day before the event. She knows Aminata works long hours but insists it is a family duty. Aminata had planned to use that Sunday to study for her accounting exam, which is in two weeks. The ceremony is important in their culture, and refusing might be seen as disrespectful. Aminata must decide whether to help her cousin or stick to her study plan.
state_and_available_memories:
Aminata worked a ten-hour shift Saturday hauling bricks and arrived home aching, with only four hours of sleep after studying until midnight. She has a practice accounting exam scheduled for Monday evening and still needs to master depreciation calculations, which she finds difficult. Her fund for her sister's relocation is exactly on track, and she fears any disruption.

The baby wrapped in Fatoumata's arms triggers a memory of Aminata at twelve, holding her own infant sister outside the hospital while her mother was dying inside—a day she was pulled from school and never fully returned. Fatoumata's tone as she says 'family duty' evokes a recollection of her father selling his trowel set to pay for that funeral, a tool she now uses every day.

She recalls her mother often saying 'We must show up for family, or we lose them,' but also remembers how her mother's constant attendance at community ceremonies left her stall unattended and accounts neglected, leading to the miscalculated loan. Aminata has internalized that counting and preparation protect against the same faith in goodwill that ruined her family.
name: Aminata Diallo
